title: Nexwall Endpoint 0.1.0-dev1
summary: First development preview: enrolment with a tenant-bound identity, an ingest service that rejects cross-tenant events, and the OCSF event model. Not for production; there is no download yet.
overview: Nexwall Endpoint is the endpoint detection and response product of Nexwall, built to work together with Nexwall Firewall. This first development preview contains the foundations only: how an endpoint proves who it is, how its events reach the service, and how events are described. It is a lab build for the development team and is not available for download.

at_a_glance.label: Endpoint systems tested
at_a_glance.value: Windows 10 22H2 and Linux x86-64, in the lab

sections.title: What is new
sections.intro: Everything in this preview is new.

items.title: Enrolment with a single-use token
items.body: An administrator creates a one-time token for a tenant. The agent generates its own key on the endpoint, sends a certificate request with the token, and receives a certificate signed by the Nexwall Endpoint certificate authority.
bullets: The private key never leaves the endpoint.
The tenant and the device are written into the certificate by the service; nothing in the request can choose them.
A token works once and expires; a reused or unknown token is refused.
Verified end to end on Windows 10 and Linux.

items.title: Tenant isolation at ingest
items.body: Events are accepted over mutual TLS (TLS 1.3). The tenant and the device come only from the certificate. An event that names another tenant or device is rejected with 403, and the request size is limited to 1 MiB.

items.title: OCSF 1.10.0 event model
items.body: Every event is wrapped in a versioned envelope and described with the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework, version 1.10.0. This preview maps process, file, network and DNS activity. The class numbers are pinned and checked by the tests.

items.title: Windows sensor verified in the lab
items.body: On a Windows 10 22H2 lab machine with Defender on, 11 stock behaviour rules of the Windows sensor fired as expected. A 25-minute soak test ran 115 loops with no crash and a peak of 121 MB of memory.
items.note: Lab results on one operating system; the wider matrix is still to be tested.

items.title: Batch ingestion
items.body: The agent sends events to the Controller in batches of up to 50. The Controller refuses a whole batch if any event in it names another tenant or device than the certificate, so nothing from a refused batch is stored. If the Controller is unreachable the events stay on disk and are delivered later; an event the Controller refuses for good is counted and skipped without blocking the others.

items.title: Staged updates (agent side)
items.body: The agent can verify a signed update manifest, refuse an older one, place each device in a canary, early or general ring, install only after checking size and SHA-256, check that the new version is healthy, and go back to the previous version if it is not. A stop switch from the Controller holds every device, and an older manifest cannot lift it.
items.note: The update service and the installers are not built yet; this preview has the agent logic only.

items.title: Certificate renewal and revocation
items.body: Agent certificates are short-lived. The agent renews its certificate before it expires and rotates its key at the same time, without a restart. An administrator can revoke a single device or a whole tenant; a revoked identity is refused immediately on every route, including renewal, even though its certificate has not yet expired.
bullets: The key and certificate are replaced as a pair, and an interrupted renewal is repaired at the next start.
Events queued on a revoked device are kept, not discarded.

items.title: Tamper-evident audit log
items.body: Enrolments, certificate renewals, revocations and update releases are written to an append-only log in which every record includes the hash of the previous one. Editing, deleting, inserting or reordering records is detected, and signed checkpoints detect a log that was cut short. If a record cannot be written, the action is refused.
items.note: Checkpoint signing with a managed key and a tenant-facing view of the log are not built yet.

items.title: Update service
items.body: The Controller signs update manifests and serves the update files. A release is opened ring by ring (canary, early, general), and a stop switch halts one release stream or all of them at once. A stop cannot be undone by replaying an older manifest.
items.note: In this preview the update is applied by a generic file installer in the lab; installers that replace the running agent on Windows, Linux and macOS are not built yet.

items.title: Durable event pipeline
items.body: Events accepted by the Controller are published to a message bus (NATS JetStream) before the agent is told they were accepted, so an accepted event is on disk. The tenant and device are taken from the certificate and written into every event. An indexer stores events in a separate area for each tenant and moves any message whose content does not match its tenant to a quarantine instead of storing it. An agent that resends the same event does not create a duplicate.
items.note: This preview stores events in files for development. Search and analytics stores (OpenSearch, ClickHouse) are not built yet.

items.title: Stricter tenant checks on events
items.body: An event that carries its own tenant or device field is accepted only if it matches the certificate exactly. Empty or malformed values and keys that differ only in letter case are refused, and a refused event is reported as a permanent error so the agent does not retry it forever. Certificate names must be in one exact form. A new randomised cross-tenant test and fuzz tests now run against these paths.
items.note: Found during testing: no customer data was involved.

items.title: Sensors run as separate programs
items.body: The agent can now start and supervise sensors that run as their own programs and talk to it over a local channel (a Unix socket, or a named pipe on Windows). Events from a sensor travel through the agent to the Controller, and each sensor receives its own part of the signed policy when it connects and whenever the policy changes. If a sensor refuses a policy, the agent rolls the whole policy back. A small test sensor is included for labs.
items.note: The Windows, Linux and macOS production sensors are not connected yet; only the test sensor uses this path today.

items.title: More event types in the common format
items.body: Events can now describe registry key and value changes, modules (DLLs and libraries) being loaded or unloaded, memory operations between processes, sign-ins and sign-outs, and detection findings with the rule and the MITRE ATT&CK technique that raised them. They use the same open schema (OCSF 1.10.0) as process, file, network and DNS events, so they can be searched and correlated together.
items.note: The sensors that produce these events are still being connected; the format is ready for them.

items.title: Signed policies with rollback
items.body: The Controller signs each policy; the agent verifies the signature, refuses older revisions than the one it already runs, applies the policy module by module, and goes back to the last known good policy if a module fails to apply or fails its health check. The agent then reports whether it complies.
bullets: Keys can be rotated without re-enrolling.
Each tenant has its own policy and its own revision counter.
Verified on Windows 10 and Linux, including a wrong-key refusal.

items.title: Sensor channel
items.body: Detection sensors run as separate processes and send events to the agent over a local channel that only the system and administrators can open. If the agent restarts it asks the sensor to resume after the last event it received, and lost events are counted.

items.title: Durable event queue
items.body: Events wait on disk until the Controller confirms them, so a restart or a network outage does not lose them. The queue has a size limit; when it is full the oldest events are dropped and the number dropped is counted. Damaged records are detected and skipped.

items.title: Licence check in every build
items.body: Each build scans its dependencies and fails when a licence is incompatible with the product, and keeps a record of where every detection rule and component comes from.

entries.title: Batch ingestion and update logic
entries.text: The agent run loop, batch ingestion and the staged-update logic, verified on Windows 10 and Linux.

entries.title: Renewal, revocation, audit log, update service
entries.text: Certificate renewal and revocation, the tamper-evident audit log and the Controller update service, verified end to end.

entries.title: Policies, sensor channel and event queue
entries.text: Signed policy pull with rollback, the local sensor channel and the durable event queue, verified on Windows 10 and Linux.

entries.title: More event types
entries.text: Registry, module, memory, sign-in and detection-finding events in the OCSF 1.10.0 format.

entries.title: Sensors as separate programs
entries.text: The agent supervises sensor processes over a local channel; events and per-sensor policy cross the process boundary.

entries.title: Stricter tenant checks
entries.text: Events must match the certificate identity exactly; look-alike fields are refused; cross-tenant and fuzz tests added.

entries.title: Durable event pipeline
entries.text: Events are persisted on a message bus before acceptance, and indexed per tenant with quarantine for mismatches.

entries.title: First development preview
entries.text: Enrolment, tenant-bound ingest and the first OCSF mappers, verified on Windows 10 22H2 and Linux.

requirements: There is nothing to install yet: the preview is not published for download.
Later releases will state the supported Windows, Linux and macOS versions here.
upgrade: There is no upgrade path yet. Development previews are not meant to be installed by customers.
open_source: Nexwall Endpoint combines open-source components with Nexwall code. The list of components, versions and licences will be published with the first release, together with the software bill of materials. Every build already runs a licence check.
